title: Most Folks Only Figure Out How Their Septic System Works… Once It Stops Working

segments.title: Cold Open (Hook)
imagery: Late evening. Colonial house near the woods. Soft moonlight.
Camera pulls back toward the new garage.
Grass around the garage glows unnatural bright green in a clean rectangular shape.
Family and Mr. Pipes stand in silence; only silhouettes visible.
Camera slowly pushes in on the glowing grass.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: Most folks only figure out how their septic system really works… once it stops working.

segments.title: Introduction
imagery: Mr. Pipes stands in his workshop. Clean, well-lit space.
Tools and spare parts on the wall behind him.
Friendly, easygoing expression straight at camera.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Hey there, I'm Mr. Pipes. I install and service septic systems and heating around this part of the country.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Today I want to tell you a story I run into more often than you'd think. A good family who tried to do everything right… and still managed to get almost everything wrong without even realizing it.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: We're gonna walk through what happened, and I'll explain along the way why each little decision mattered.

segments.title: Scene 1 – The Welcome
imagery: Bright sunny afternoon. Three-story colonial house near the trees.
Moving truck just pulling away.
Mr. Pipes walks up the gravel driveway with a clipboard.
Homeowner steps out — broad-shouldered, jeans, flannel shirt, cowboy hat.
Wife in practical dress and three kids stand behind him.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Afternoon! Name's Pipes. The county's running sewer lines out this way. Just wanted to see if y'all were interested in a quote to hook up.

dialogue.speaker: dad
dialogue.text: Appreciate the offer, but this place has been handling things the old-fashioned way for a hundred years. All natural. Self-contained. No monthly bills, no city nonsense. Already saved us a few thousand bucks right there.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Fair enough. You know where to find me if anything ever comes up.

segments.title: Scene 2 – Dinner & the Disposal
imagery: Warm kitchen light in the evening. Family around a big wooden table.
Teenage daughter pushes her plate away.
Mom scrapes leftovers straight into the sink and hits the garbage disposal.
Deep, strained grrrrnnnk from the pipes. Everybody freezes half a second, then life continues.

segments.title: Education 1 – Garbage Disposals
imagery: Clean animated cross-section of a septic tank.
Food scraps dropping into the tank and joining the sludge layer.
Arrow showing sludge moving toward the outlet.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: A garbage disposal feels handy, but every time you grind up food scraps, you're sending solid material straight into the septic tank. That tank is built to let solids settle out. Food waste piles a lot more sludge in there than the system was designed for. Over time that sludge layer gets higher and higher. Once it reaches the outlet, it starts heading into the drainfield. And once solids get into the soil, they clog it for good. That's why most of us in the business say: use the disposal as little as possible… or better yet, not at all.

segments.title: Scene 3 – The Diaper
imagery: Bathroom. Mom finishes changing the baby, rolls up the dirty diaper, drops it in the toilet.
Water rises higher than normal and drains reluctantly.
Mom pours CAUSTIC drain cleaner. Blob… blob… gurgle. Water goes down.

segments.title: Education 2 – Flushing Diapers
imagery: Toilet → pipe → tank.
The diaper stays whole and gets stuck near the outlet baffle.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: Only two things should ever go down a toilet on a septic system: human waste and toilet paper. Diapers, wipes, paper towels — even the ones that say 'flushable' — don't break down the way regular toilet paper does. They stay in one piece, catch on the baffles, and create blockages. What looks like it flushed is often still sitting in the tank or starting to slow everything down.

segments.title: Education 3 – Harsh Chemicals
imagery: Bacteria symbols inside the tank fade after the chemical is poured in.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: When the water starts draining slow, a lot of folks reach for a strong drain cleaner. Those products are made for regular house plumbing. In a septic tank they kill the good bacteria that break down the waste. A septic system is a living biological process. When you hit it with caustic chemicals, that process slows way down or stops.

segments.title: Scene 4 – Next Morning Problem
imagery: Bright morning light. Hallway and living room.
Middle kid comes out of the bathroom.
Dad grabs the truck keys and heads out.

dialogue.speaker: mid_child
dialogue.text: Mom, the toilet won't flush right.

dialogue.speaker: mom
dialogue.text: Just put a little more of that drain cleaner in it.

dialogue.speaker: dad
dialogue.text: No way. This is a living system. It needs the right bacteria, not more chemicals. I'm going to get some proper additives.

segments.title: Scene 5 – At Mr. Pipes' Shop
imagery: Clean, practical workshop.
Dad walks in looking a little stressed.
Mr. Pipes calmly wiping his hands.

dialogue.speaker: dad
dialogue.text: I need those septic additives. Something to get the digestion going again.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Sure, I carry those. But before we go that route… mind if I take a quick look at the system first? Sometimes it's easier to see what's actually going on.

segments.title: Scene 6 – The Questions on the Property
imagery: Mr. Pipes walks the yard with the whole family.
Dad gets more defensive.
Dad points toward the new garage and the deep-green grass.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: When was the tank last pumped since y'all moved in?

dialogue.speaker: dad
dialogue.text: Shouldn't have been that long ago…

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Do you know exactly where the tank and the drainfield are located?

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: Has anybody built or driven over the field area?

dialogue.speaker: dad
dialogue.text: Look at the grass around the garage — real deep green. That means the system is feeding the lawn. It's healthy.

segments.title: Education 4 – The Additives Myth
imagery: Sludge filling the tank higher and higher.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: Additives can't remove the sludge that's already sitting in the tank. The only way to get that material out is to pump it. Relying on additives usually just puts off the day the tank finally overflows into the drainfield.

segments.title: Education 5 – Building or Driving on the Drainfield
imagery: Soil getting compacted under a garage foundation.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: Heavy weight — whether it's a building or vehicles — compacts the soil. Once that soil is packed down, water can't move through it the way it's supposed to. Pipes can get crushed too. And when the field fails, the building is sitting right on top of the problem.

segments.title: Education 6 – The Green Grass Warning
imagery: Effluent rising toward the surface and turning the grass unnaturally green.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: Really lush, deep-green grass in one specific area isn't a sign the system is fertilizing the lawn. Most of the time it means effluent is rising up close to the surface instead of being properly absorbed and treated underground.

segments.title: Scene 7 – The Reveal
imagery: Evening light fading. Family and Mr. Pipes at the new garage.
Grass glowing unnatural bright green in a perfect rectangular shape matching a drainfield.
Long quiet moment. Camera slowly circles the glowing patch.
Family faces as it sinks in.

segments.title: Positive Section – What a Healthy Approach Looks Like
imagery: Mr. Pipes back on camera.
Clean checklist appears one item at a time.
Simple, positive animations of a healthy system.

vo.speaker: mr_pipes
vo.text: None of these problems happen overnight. They build up from a bunch of little everyday decisions that feel harmless at the time. Good news is, most of them are completely avoidable once you understand how the system actually works. Here's what a healthy approach looks like: Know exactly where your tank and drainfield are. Get the tank pumped on a regular schedule. Keep the surface of the drainfield clear and protected. Be careful what goes down the drains. Call a pro when something feels off. A septic system is tough and can last decades… if you treat it like the living system it is.

checklist.item: Know exactly where your tank and drainfield are
Get the tank pumped on a regular schedule
Keep the surface of the drainfield clear and protected
Be careful what goes down the drains
Call a pro when something feels off

segments.title: Closing
imagery: Mr. Pipes standing in front of his service truck or workshop. Warm light.
Company logo fades in softly.
End card with logo, simple contact line, and a soft subscribe prompt.

dialogue.speaker: mr_pipes
dialogue.text: If you're not sure where your system is, or if the grass is looking a little too healthy in one spot — it's worth a conversation. I'm local. Happy to help.
